title: Super savings in AI criminals' sights
full_text:
Breakthroughs in AI have helped fuel an 80 per cent surge in attacks on businesses and government agencies by criminals and countries such as China and Russia amid warnings the new technology could be used to wipe out people's superannuation savings.
In its annual assessment of cyber threats, to be released today, the Australian Signals Directorate says the nature and speed of attacks has changed sharply since the emergence of so-called "frontier" AI this year, jeopardising businesses and the economy.
Frontier AI models, such as the latest and most advanced versions of artificial intelligence like Anthropic's Mythos, deliver complex problem-solving and advanced scientific modelling but they have also been used to identify vulnerabilities in computer software.
The technology uncovered vulnerabilities in the computer programming language PHP that forced websites offline last week for patching, including at the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
ASD director-general Abigail Bradshaw said that while AI had enabled agencies such as hers to identify and take swift action against cyberattacks, it was also being used by criminals and bad actors to mount more dangerous digital assaults.
"[Frontier AI is] creating enormous opportunities, but they are also enabling malicious cyber actors to identify vulnerabilities and conduct attacks faster, at a greater scale and with the greater precision than ever before. This shift will only accelerate," she said.
"As the global security environment remains challenging, state-sponsored cyber actors will increasingly leverage AI to enhance the scale, speed and effectiveness of their operations."
Australian Prudential Regulation Authority deputy chairman David Bradbury told The Australian Financial Review's Super and Wealth Summit yesterday that the risk posed by cyberattacks kept him awake at night. "It's important that we're ensuring that members' best interests are being observed, but when you're talking about things like a cyberattack that might be amplified by AI, driven by foreign actors; something like this could actually start to clean out people's accounts," he said.
Australian superannuation funds hold more than $4.5 trillion in assets in at least 25 million accounts.
In the 2025-26 financial year, the ASD notified companies and agencies more than 4400 times of potentially malicious cyber activity, an 80 per cent jump on the previous year.
The agency responded to more than 1500 incidents in 2025-26 - up from the 1200 in 2024-25.
It received more than 82,000 cybercrime reports; it, blocked customer access to more than 564 million malicious website domains; and it responded to 139 ransomware incidents.
The cost to businesses from cyberattacks continues to grow, climbing 16 per cent last year to an average $93,500 for self-reported cases. Attacks on medium-sized businesses jumped by 45 per cent to an average cost of $141,300.
A continuing issue is the wide use of "legacy" software and hardware by businesses and government agencies that is too old to be updated to deal with increasingly sophisticated attacks.
Bradshaw urged firms and agencies to update their cyber protections, even if it meant shutting down an online presence temporarily to safeguard their operations.
"Organisations must take action to improve basic cyber hygiene. System security must be prioritised over system availability in order to deal with increased vulnerability discovery by AI models," she said. "The less legacy technology exposed to the internet, the fewer opportunities malicious actors have to gain access."
Membership of the Five Eyes group of intelligence-sharing nations that includes the US, Britain, Canada and New Zealand has enabled Australia to keep using Mythos, an AI agent deemed so powerful the Trump administration has clamped down on access.
A key concern remains state-sponsored actors, largely from China and Russia, trying to gain access to sensitive or private information. In some cases, they seek to learn how a business or agency works or they gather information that fills their own intelligence gaps.
Defence Minister Richard Marles said in a statement that the risk of cyber incidents had increased substantially.
"To stay ahead, Australians must enhance their cyber defences," he said.
